It is celebrated in the Tirap district of Arunachal Pradesh by the Nocte tribe in July/August. The word 'Lofe ' (from which Loku is derived) means "to drive out" (driving out the old season). It is a 3-day harvest festival celebrated around Oct-Nov at the end of the paddy harvest. Day 1 (Famlam): "Famlam" involves omen-reading by elders to determine jhum plots before the buffalo slaughter begins. This is the day when the ceremonial animal slaughter (pigs, buffaloes) actually takes place. Day 2 (Chamkatja): People visit monasteries or shrines ('Chaatam ') to offer prayers. Day 3 (Thanglangja): This is the farewell day involving communal dancing, fasting, and omen-reading.
New Year Festival of Tibetan Buddhism, celebrated by the Monpa tribe. It marks the 1st day of the Tibetan calendar.
Celebrated by the Galo tribe in April. Popir Dance is performed during the Mopin festival.
To honour the war heroes who died in WW2.
Founded in 2012. It is celebrated in the Ziro Valley.
celebrated by the Nyishi tribe in Spring/Feb.
It is celebrated by the Apatani tribe in the Ziro Valley. This festival is based on rotating village responsibility for rituals.

Celebrated by the Nyishi tribe in Feb. It refers to the ritual invocation (prayer) of deities for harmony and prosperity, where Nyo means earth, Kum means Collectiveness and Yullo means invocation. It is an agricultural festival where Donyi-Polo (the Moon/Sun God) is worshipped for a bountiful harvest.

Celebrated by the Tutsa tribe. It is primarily observed to seek blessings from the Rangkhothak deity before millet harvesting. "Pongtu " translates to " retreating wind". It is a pre-harvest festival and is also celebrated as a New Year festival.

Celebrated thrice a year: Rongali/ Bohag Bihu(April): Assam New Year Kati/Kongali Bihu (Oct-Nov) Bhogali/Magh Bihu (Jan) Uruka before Magh Bihu features bonfires and feasting. Manuh Bihu includes gifting Gamucha and traditional dishes.
Pre-harvest festival celebrated by the Rabha Community in June, featuring the 'Baranakai' fire.
The New Year festival of the Bodo Kachari community is celebrated in Mid-April, where prayers are offered to 'Bathou' / Lord Shiva.
A 3-day annual festival held in January at Lekhapani in Tinsukia district.
Harvest festival of the Mishing Tribe. Seed sowing festival in Feb-March by the Mising tribe, featuring the 'Gumrag' dance.

Held at Kamakhya temple. Marks the Menstrual phase of Goddess Kamakhya. Also known as Ameti/Tantric fertility festival. It occurs around mid-June and signifies the onset of the monsoon. The word 'Ambubachi' means " spoken with water ". It symbolizes Mother Earth regaining her fertility (rejuvenating for agriculture). For 3 days, the land is left completely empty - no digging, plowing, or sowing is allowed.
A 3-day festival held in November.
Celebrated by the Karbi tribe.
Exchange of products through Barter exchange.
Known as Magh Bihu or Bhogali Bihu.
Dimasa community
The largest fair for elephant trading in Asia is actually the Sonepur Mela, which is held in November in Patna, Bihar.
Originates from the Mithila region.

It is a major festival of Bihar and UP dedicated to "Chhathi Maiya" and the Sun God (Surya). It begins exactly on the 6th day after Diwali. It is a 4-day long festival celebrated during Kartik month (around Oct / Nov).
Celebrated in August, devotees pray to the Serpent Goddess Mansa.
A 3 day festival started in 1986.

It is celebrated in the Mithila region of Bihar. This festival honors Baba Salhesh, who belonged to the Dusadh Dalit community. The Dusadh Dalit community is the primary group that celebrates this. The 'Bhagat' and 'Manarias ' narrate the dramatic stories and legends of Baba Salhesh.
Known as Khichdi.

The Santhal community is mainly found in the states of Jharkhand, Bihar, Odisha, and West Bengal. Erok Sim marks the 'beginning' of the agricultural season. It is a seed-sowing festival celebrated before the sowing of paddy crops, very similar to the Chapchar Kut festival of Mizoram. Erok Sim is also known by the names 'Harisim' or 'Harpod'. Magh Sim is celebrated to express gratitude for the harvest and to prepare for a new agricultural cycle. During these festivals, animal sacrifices are made by the Santhal community, which generally consist of a rooster / chicken. The sacrifice is performed by the village priest, who is known as the 'Naike' (or Naiki). The sacrifice is offered at a sacred grove (a sacred piece of land/forest) known as the 'Jaherthan'. The deities to whom these sacrifices are offered are named 'Jaher Era'and 'Marang Buru'. Chhattisgarh

It is celebrated on the eve of Holi in the Dantewada district of Chhattisgarh. It is celebrated by the Gond and Baiga tribes during February-March (the month of Phagun). It takes place at the Maa Danteshwari temple and is also referred to as the "Kumbh Mela of Tribal Culture".

The Chariot festival is celebrated in Bastar (Jagdalpur), Chhattisgarh, primarily by the Maria and Muria tribe for 9 days. It marks the beginning of the famous Bastar Dussehra (which lasts for 75 days). Tupki is a playful mock gun made of wood/bamboo that uses Goncha fruits as bullets. A chariot procession takes place during the months of June-July, a tradition started by the Chalukya rulers. Rath Yatra begins on Ashadh Shukla Dashmi and ends on Dutiya.

A thanks giving festival to acknowledge the importance of Bulls & Oxen. It is celebrated in Madhya Pradesh (Balaghat), Maharashtra, and Chhattisgarh. It takes place during the month of Shravan (monsoon) on an Amavasya (New Moon) night. After completing the heavy field work (plowing/sowing), farmers bathe and decorate their bulls with oil, turmeric, and paints to honor their hard work.
A Harvest festival of Shravan month (July/August) celebrated by farmers.
To honour Goddess Danteshwari.
A harvest festival tribute to Karam Tree.
An annual fair held in Champaran region, Raipur.
Muria tribe
Also known as the Epiphany festival.
Celebrated on 3rd December (Death anniversary of Saint Francis). It takes place at the Basilica of Bom Jesus (associated with St. Francis Xavier).
Wine festival
Celebrated immediately before the Lent Christian period.
Asia's largest Electronic Dance Music festival.

Shigmotsav/ Shishirotsava is a spring festival celebrated in Falgun month of the Hindu calendar. Shigmo is celebrated in the spring season for 14 days to welcome homecoming warriors. The Ghode Modni (warrior dance) and Fugdi dance (performed to the beat of drums) are performed during this festival.
Celebrated on the 4th Saturday of every August in the Divar Island.
A mud festival that celebrates Lord Krishna's childhood, in the Devaki Krishna temple of Marcel, Goa.
Saint John the Baptist festival.
Dedicated to Lord Vishnu. Celebrated for 3 weeks in November.
Celebrates the marriage of Lord Krishna and Rukmini in the Porbandar district of Gujarat.
Celebrated at Modhera Sun temple (Mehsana district) for 3 days in the 3rd week of January.
An animal trading festival.
Also known as the "White Desert Festival", it continues for 3 months in the Great Rann of Kutch.
A tribal festival celebrated just before Holi.
Gharasia/Bhil tribe
Dedicated to Lord Shiva.
Dedicated to Mekaran Dada (a famous saint of Kutch).
Uttarayan (famous for the International Kite Festival).
It is celebrated in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. It lasts for 13 days. Indian classical music is showcased in this festival. Himachal Pradesh
Also known as the Horse Festival.
It is celebrated in the Lahaul Valley. It takes place around the time of Magh Purnima (Jan-feb). It is a 2-day New Year festival celebration for the locals in this region.
Festival of flowers. Also known as the Ukyam Festival. It takes place in the Kinnaur district of Himachal Pradesh. It is celebrated in the month of Bhadrapad (August- September).
Celebrated in the Kinnaur Valley. Sair festival.
Held in the town of Chamba for one week. A week-long Festival is celebrated in Chamba Valley during July–August and marks the onset of the monsoon, where a masked dance known as "Cham" is performed.
Losar is the Tibetan New Year, famously known for its mask dances, which are called "Cham ". Celebrated in the Lahaul Spiti Valley.
Dedicated to Lord Raghunath.

It is also known as the Hidimba Devi Fair, in honor of Hidimba Devi (wife of Bhima). It is celebrated in the spring season (around March) for 3 days. It takes place in the Kullu valley or Manali in Himachal Pradesh.
It takes place in Bilaspur, Himachal Pradesh. It lasts for 4 to 5 days and is held at the Luhnu ground. It is primarily a cattle fair.
Punha involves symbolic ploughing indoors using willow sticks, reflecting farming hopes during snow. Celebrated in Pattan Valley.

A 5,000-year-old traditional, masked cultural festival. It is celebrated in Kalpa and Kinnaur district of Himachal Pradesh honoring Sauni (mountain fairies) who protect villagers during harsh winter. The festival welcomes spring, marks the end of winter, and centers on a symbolic, silent divine marriage involving two villagers-the Raula and Raulane-representing celestial beings.
A festival celebrated in Sirmaur district during March-April, known as the "Festival of Pictures," where traditional dishes like Potlu are prepared.
An international crafts fair held in Faridabad, Haryana.
Held in Panchkula district.
Dedicated to Gugga Pir, worship of snakes.
Dedicated to Goddess Gauri or Parvati. Also celebrated in Rajasthan & MP.
It marks the beginning of the sowing season.
To honour Budha Baba celebrated by indigenous tribes of Jharkhand.
A Harvest festival is celebrated on the new moon day of Kartik. Cattle Worship is the primary focus of the Sohrai festival.
Held on the last day of Hindu month Paush.
To honour Karam Devta-God of Power and Youthfulness, for a good harvest. During the Karam festival, a Karam tree is worshipped.
Marks the arrival of Spring.

Celebrated by unmarried tribal girls for fertility and good agricultural prosperity. Grains (like barley/jau) are planted in a pot of soil, and as they sprout, they are called 'Jawa'. Both Karam and Jawa are celebrated around the monsoon season, generally in the Bhadrapada month (August-September).
Erok Sim & Magh Sim festivals. The Santhal community is mainly found in the states of Jharkhand, Bihar, Odisha, and West Bengal.
Also known as "Vijay Utsav".
A buffalo race event.

Held every 12 years Anointment of the Bahubali Gommateshwara statue, located at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka. Celebrated by the Jain community for Bahubali (son of Rishabhanatha), at Shravanabelagola where his largest statue (~57 ft monolithic) is located; last held in 2018, next in 2030.
A cultural festival held in January at Pattadakal, showcasing classical dance forms.
Worship of arms and weapons, celebrated by the Kodava community of Kodagu district.
Known as the "Festival of Dolls". Dolls are placed in odd numbers (usually 9) since it is associated with the Navratri and Dussehra period in Karnataka.
Words ending with "Habba " generally belong to Karnataka. It is celebrated with the worship of Godess Gouri and is observed one day before Ganesh Chaturthi
New Year Festival.

It is one of the oldest festivals of Bengaluru, celebrated in March–April. It is celebrated in Tamil Nadu & Karnataka. The festival lasts for 11 days. It is celebrated by the Thigala community to honor Draupadi and Shakti.

The Kodava community of Karnataka primarily celebrates three main festivals. 1. Puthari:
It is the harvest festival (also known as the new rice festival), generally celebrated around December.
The traditional dance performed during this time is called "Ummathat".
The chant "Poli, Poli, Deva" translates to "Increase, Increase, O God." where people pray to God for an abundant harvest. 2. Kailpodh:
A festival dedicated to weapon worship (weapons are worshipped during this time).
It generally takes place around September. 3. Kaveri Sankramana:
A river worship festival dedicated to the Kaveri River, generally taking place around October.
A religious fair held at Badami, dedicated to Banashankari Devi.
Celebrated in Thrissur during April-May at the Vadakkumnathan temple. It is known as the "Festival of Festivals".
Vishu is a New Year festival of Kerala that falls in the month of Medam (mid-April).
Celebrated mostly in North Malabar.
Held at Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple.

Holds the record for the largest gathering of women for a religious purpose. It is celebrated in Thiruvananthapuram for 10 days. It is known as the "Sabarimala of Women" because women are not allowed in the Sabarimala temple, whereas only women celebrate Attukal Pongala.
Celebrated at Padmanabha Swamy temple.
The Vallamkali boat race takes place during the Onam festival in Kerala. The boats used in this traditional race are snake-shaped.
A Harvest festival welcomes the return of the demon King Mahabali. Onam is the biggest festival of Kerala, held in Aug-Sept (Bhadrapada month).
Held at Sabarimala temple, dedicated to Lord Ayyappa.
A week-long dance festival is held in the last week of January, every year.

It is dedicated to honoring Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati. It marks the union of Lord Shiva and Parvati, specifically the day Lord Shiva accepted Parvati as his wife. A central lamp is placed, and women wearing white sarees perform a dance around it. It is celebrated mainly in the Malayalam month of Dhanu (December-January).
This is a local name for Holi in Kerala. It is primarily celebrated by the Kudumbi and Konkani communities of Kerala.

It is a 10-day annual festival held at the Sri Krishna Temple. It takes place around February-March (Chaitra month). It begins with an elephant race known as 'Aanayottam'. It concludes with 'Aarattu', which is a holy immersion ceremony.

It is also known as the 'Feast of Christ the King'. It is celebrated by the Christian community. It is a 10-day annual celebration held at the Madre De Deus Church in Vettukad, Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala.
It is an 11-day annual festival. It takes place at the Beemapally Dargah Shareef (Masjid) in Thiruvananthapuram. It is organized in honor of Saint Beema Beevi and her son.
Celebrated in the month of Aug-Sept.
Commences on Republic Day.
Held in Chhatarpur district.
Celebrated by Baigas of Mandla district.
A 6-day festival.

Celebrated in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh during March-April. Dedicated to Mata Gauri (an incarnation of Goddess Parvati). Ghudliya: It is the decorated earthen pot with a lamp inside that unmarried girls carry. Purpose: Unmarried girls pray for a good husband, while married women pray for the long life and well-being of their families.
To worship the relics of Sariputta and Mahamogallena, in Sanchi, MP.
A harvest festival in the spring season.

It is celebrated in Madhya Pradesh (Balaghat), Maharashtra, and Chhattisgarh. It takes place during the month of Shravan (monsoon) on an Amavasya (New Moon) night. After completing the heavy field work (plowing/sowing), farmers bathe and decorate their bulls with oil, turmeric, and paints to honor their hard work.
The fair is held during the months of April and May. It takes place at the dargah of Sufi saint Mastan Shah Vali located in Sagar, Madhya Pradesh.
It is celebrated by the Bhil & Gond tribe of MP and Chhattisgarh. Known as the "100-drum festival". It features a ceremonial pig wedding in honour of Narayana Dev.
The ceremonial procession of Lord Dharanath in the Dhar district of Madhya Pradesh is locally referred to as a Chhabina.
Manipur
A Hindu festival of Manipur associated with Lord Jagannath Rath Yatra, celebrated for 10 days.

It is popularly known as the Holi of Manipur. It is a Spring festival that lasts for about 5 days. It is celebrated on the full moon day of the Lamta month (February-March). The festival features sports competitions, not academic quiz competitions. Thabal Chongba is a moonlight circle dance performed during this festival.

It is called the "Merry-making of Gods," celebrated by the Meitei community. It involves the worship of Umang Lai (ancestral forest deities). Male priests are called 'Maibas' and female priests are 'Maibis'. The Khamba Thoibi dance is also performed during this time.
It is a boat racing festival.
It is a seed-sowing festival (marking the beginning of the agricultural season) celebrated by the Naga tribes of Manipur around December-January.
It is a post-harvest thanksgiving festival celebrated by the Zeliangrong Naga community of Manipur.
Focuses on the role of women in society and involves inviting sisters for feasting and gifts.
The New Year of the Meitei community, occurring in March-April.

It is also known as Kwak Tanba. It is celebrated in Manipur by the Meitei community. It is also called the 'Crow Festival' because a crow was released from the king's palace during this festival. It marks the end of the monsoon season and the beginning of prosperity. The monsoon ends around September-October, which is why it is celebrated in October. Nagaland

Known for showcasing tribal culture and heritage. Celebrated from 1-10 December by Naga tribes. Nagaland's biggest festival ("Festival of Festivals"). The Hornbill bird symbolizes strength and cultural unity.
It is celebrated in the 1st week of April by the Konyak Naga people.

Celebrated by the Ao Naga tribe (3 days) in the first week of May. The Ao Naga tribe serves as a time of recreation and joy after the hard work of clearing fields and sowing seeds. Sangpangtu: It is a ritual performed by the Ao tribe during the Moatsu Festival.
Celebrated by the Angami tribe to invoke prosperity and ward off evil spirits before the sowing season. Also known as Phousanyi, it takes place in February for purifying the body and soul.
The mid-July harvest festival of the Sumi tribe.
It is a pre-harvest festival held in early August (for 3 days).
The post-harvest festival of the Lotha tribe that lasts for 9 days.
It is celebrated for 10 days by the Pochury tribe. It takes place in February and marks the beginning of the agricultural season. 'Khupielilie' dance is specifically performed during this festival.

It is celebrated by the Dimasa Kachari tribe in Nagaland (and Assam). It is a post-harvest festival (celebrated after the crop harvest). It takes place in the month of January, and the deity Sibrai is worshipped during this time.

An agriculture festival where new rice is offered as Prasad. This newly harvested rice is specifically offered to Maa Samaleswari in Sambalpur, Odisha. In the local language, "Nua" means new, and "Khai" means food. "Nabanna" refers to the newly harvested rice. The famous "Dalkhai" dance is performed to celebrate this festival.
A 5-day dance festival held Dec 1-5.
2-day long event. Martial arts and dance.

Also known as Mithun Sankranti. It can be related to the Ambubachi festival of Assam. The land is left completely empty for three days. No sowing, digging, or playing takes place during this period. It is believed that Goddess Earth is regaining her fertility during this time.
The chariot journey of Lord Jagannath, Balabhadra, and Subhadra.
Celebrated in Jagannath Temple.
This festival is celebrated in the Koraput region of Odisha. It takes place during the month of Chaitra (February-March). It is associated with Dhemsa dances and drum performances.
Erok Sim & Magh Sim festivals. The Santhal community is mainly found in the states of Jharkhand, Bihar, Odisha, and West Bengal.
A festival of the Khasi tribe known as the "Dance of Peaceful Hearts" and celebrated in the spring season (April), lasting for 3 days.
A 5-day harvest festival that takes place in Autumn (Oct-Nov), celebrated by the Khasi tribe.

The monsoon (July) festival of the Jaintia (Pnar) tribe lasts for 3 days. "Behdien" means to drive away, and "Khlam" means plague (driving away the plague). Therefore, this festival was initially started to drive away plagues or evil diseases.

Garo Tribe (aka Festival of Festivals). It involves the worship of the Sun, the Earth, and agricultural tools to ensure a bountiful harvest. It is celebrated by the Garo tribe and is also known as the "Festival of 100 Drums".
Held in Ri-Bhoi district.
Held in Shillong.

It is celebrated as a thanksgiving festival to God after the harvesting season. It is both a dance and a festival. It is celebrated by the Garo, Khasi, and Jaintia (Pnar) tribes of Meghalaya during the harvest season.
It is celebrated by the Garo tribe of Meghalaya. It is a spring festival and an agricultural festival that takes place around March.
A spring festival marking the preparation for maize sowing (March). "Kut" means festival in the local language. Any festival ending in Kut is generally from Mizoram.
The cultural significance of "Mim" in the Mim Kut festival is the last harvest representing survival and love.
Also known as the "Straw Festival". It is a harvest festival celebrated in December. Mim kut, Chapchar Kut and pawl Kut festivals are celebrated by the Kuki Chin-Mizo tribes.
This festival takes place in the month of March and is celebrated by the Mara tribe of Mizoram. It is celebrated after 'jhuming' (slash and burn cultivation) is completed. Festival Host: Chaypi

Begins the day after Holi (lasts for 3 days) in Anandpur Sahib. It was started by Guru Gobind Singh Ji in 1701 for training in martial arts (Gatka). It showcases martial arts, langars, and Nihang mock battles at Anandpur Sahib.
Celebrates the birth of Guru Nanak - 1st Sikh Guru. Martial arts displays by Sikhs.
Celebrated the night before Makar Sankranti (Jan 13).
Baisakhi is celebrated on 13 April, on this specific day in 1699, the 10th Sikh Guru, Guru Gobind Singh Ji, founded the Khalsa Panth (warrior clan). Marking the Sikh New Year.
A harvest festival. Lohri is celebrated a day prior.
The fair is held in Chhapar village of Ludhiana district in Punjab. It takes place in the month of September. It honors Gugga Pir, who is believed to provide protection against snakes.
Dedicated to the "Vitthal" form of Lord Vishnu.
Symbolises the victory of good over evil. The New Year of the Marathi community, where a 'Gudi' (decorated victory flag) is hoisted.
9 days long art festival.
The Koli community in Maharashtra celebrates Narali Purnima to pray for safe fishing.
It is linked to the legend of Lord Rama and the creation of a freshwater tank.
Dedicated to the legendary devotion of Savitri.

It is also known as Sharad Purnima. It is celebrated at the end of the monsoon season (in the month of Ashwin). It is celebrated by the people of Maharashtra as well as the Bengali community. In Bengali, Kojagiri means "One who is awake". People stay awake on this day because it is believed that Goddess Lakshmi arrives at night to shower blessings.
Celebrated in Bhadrapada month.

It is celebrated in Madhya Pradesh (Balaghat), Maharashtra, and Chhattisgarh. It takes place during the month of Shravan (monsoon) on an Amavasya (New Moon) night. After completing the heavy field work (plowing/sowing), farmers bathe and decorate their bulls with oil, turmeric, and paints to honor their hard work.

It is also called Hartalika Teej/Vrat, where women fast for the long life and prosperity of their husbands and children. This festival in Maharashtra involves worshipping the goddess Parvati and is considered a festival for marital bliss.

This puja is exclusively performed by married women. It is dedicated to Goddess Parvati, as "Jivati" is her incarnation. It is celebrated every Friday during the month of Shravan. The Goddess is worshipped as the life-giver and protector of children.
A camel/livestock fair held in Ajmer, Rajasthan during December that also includes religious activities.

Dedicated to Goddess Gauri. It is celebrated for 18 days. Celebrated in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh during March-April, dedicated to Mata Gauri (an incarnation of Goddess Parvati). Ghudliya: It is the decorated earthen pot with a lamp inside that unmarried girls carry. Purpose: Unmarried girls pray for a good husband, while married women pray for the long life and well-being of their families.
Celebrated in Jaisalmer, Rajasthan, for about 3 days in February.
It is also known as the Shri Ramdev Cattle Fair. It is the second-largest livestock fair, held in Nagaur, Rajasthan.
Held in Kartik month (Oct-Nov).
Held in Kartik month (Oct-Nov).
Bhil tribe Dedicated to Baneshwar Mahadev (Lord Shiva). Held in Dungarpur, Rajasthan, for 5 days. It is known as the "Kumbh of Tribals".
It is named after the great sage Kapil Muni (also called the Kapil Muni Fair). It is held in Bikaner, Rajasthan during Kartik Purnima. It includes a ritual at a lake surrounded by banyan trees.
RIFF was launched in 2007 and is recognized by UNESCO as a 'Peoples Platform'. It takes place at Mehrangarh Fort in Jodhpur. It lasts for 5 days and begins on Sharad Purnima (full moon).
It is dedicated to Lord Shree Ji and Raghunath Ji. Lord Shreeji and Raghunathji's processions on Jaljhulani Gyaras attract traders from several states.
Bhutia tribe
Lepcha tribe
Losar is the Tibetan New Year, famously known for its mask dances, which are called "Cham". It lasts for 15 days, with 3 main event days such as Lama Losar and Gyalpo Losar.
Annual 9-day festival by the Kirat Khambu Rai Community.

Chu Faat, a sacred folk dance, is performed by the Lepcha tribe of Sikkim during this festival. It signifies the worship of 5 sacred peaks: Mt. Kanchenjunga, Mt. Kabru, Mt. Simbrum, Mt. Pandim, and Mt. Narshing. It involves worship of Mount Kanchenjunga and includes prayers, masked dances and local fairs. It is also known as Pangtoed Cham and takes place in Aug-Sept. It features masked dances.
Also known as the Triple Blessed festival. Sikkim's most sacred, month-long festival that commemorates Lord Buddha's birth, enlightenment, and death (Mahaparinirvana).
Celebrated by the Lepcha community in July/August to honor Mount Tendong.
Diwali is known as Tihar in Sikkim. Sikkim's Maruni dance is performed during the Tihar festival (Diwali).
It is celebrated by the Newar (Nawar) community in Sikkim. It lasts for 8 days. It is dedicated to the Rain God (Lord Indra).
A Buddhist festival is held at Tashiding Monastery in Sikkim, where a sacred pot of holy water ("Bumchu") is opened to predict the year's fortune.
Sonam Lochar is a New Year festival of the Tamang people.
Gurung community
Celebrated in the Kumaon region.
Celebrated in the Kumaon region.

It is celebrated in a place called Dwarahat in the Almora district of Uttarakhand. It takes place at the Vimandeshwar temple in the month of Baisakh (April-May). This festival begins with the "Odha Bhetna" (stone striking) ceremony.
It marks the welcoming of the Spring season. Young girls gather first-blooming flowers and place them at the doorsteps of houses in the village to wish prosperity. It is unique to Kumaon Hills.
Celebrated on Makar Sankranti.

It is celebrated in the Chaundas Valley of Pithoragarh, Uttarakhand. It is performed by the Rung tribe. It is held once every 12 years. The festival starts with the blooming of the Kangdali plant flowers.
It is celebrated in the months of May and June and lasts for 10 days. It is celebrated because it is believed that on this day, Goddess Ganga descended from Heaven to Earth.
A week-long Jaunsari tribal fair in Chakrata thanking for harvest and honoring Santoora Devi, a Durga form.

These are associated with the Kumaon region of Uttarakhand. These Mangal geets (auspicious songs) are sung exclusively by women. They are sung during different ceremonies like childbirth, marriage, and Ganesh puja.
It is celebrated in the Kumaon region of Uttarakhand (known as Kumaoni Baithki Holi). It mainly takes place around Basant Panchami (January).
A 13-day trade fair held in Pithoragarh at the confluence of Gori River and Kali River, celebrated in November.

Pongal means "to boil". (referring to the traditional dish of boiled milk and rice). It is a harvest festival of Tamil Nadu that marks the Uttarayan (sun's northward movement / Makar Sankranti). A 4-day harvest festival (13-16 Jan): Day 1 (Bhogi): Dedicated to cleaning the home and letting go of the old. Day 2 (Thai/Surya): Dedicated to worshipping the Sun God. Day 3 (Mattu): Dedicated to worshipping Cattle. This is when the bull-taming sport Jallikattu is held. Day 4 (Kaanum): A day for family reunions and outings. Kolam: During the Pongal festival, Kolam Rangoli is drawn at the entrance of homes.
It is a traditional bull-taming event held in Tamil Nadu. It takes place during the Pongal festival, specifically on the day of Mattu Pongal (which honors cattle).
The Tamil New Year. Includes ritual baths and temple visits.
A famous annual classical dance festival in Tamil Nadu, dedicated to Lord Shiva (Nataraja), held at Chidambaram Temple, where the Cosmic dance (Tandava) of Shiva is depicted.

This festival is celebrated during November-December. It is associated with the Arunachaleshwar Temple and is generally linked to Lord Shiva. During Karthigai Deepam, earthen oil lamps called "Agal vilakku" are lit to mark the victory of good over evil.
Worship of Lord Murugan where Kavadi is carried. Celebrated on the full moon of the Tamil month Thai, it commemorates the victory of Lord Murugan over the demon Surapadma.
Known as the "Kumbh of South". Celebrated once every 12 years.
This takes place at the Arulmigu Mutharamman Temple in Tamil Nadu. It lasts for about 10 days during the Navratri period (Sept-Oct). Devotees wear demon-themed makeup and costumes.
During Thiruvathirai, women swing on mango trees to celebrate womanhood.
A turmeric bathing ceremony held when a girl achieves womanhood (first menstruation).

The Toda tribe is found in the Nilgiri Hills. Toda tribes build special huts and worship the buffalo, which is considered very sacred. "Modhwidsh" is also the New Year festival for the Toda tribe, generally celebrated around December/January.
It is celebrated mainly in Tamil Nadu and also in Karnataka. The festival lasts for 11 days. It is celebrated by the Thigala community to honor Draupadi and Shakti.
Celebrated from 17th February to 27th February.
Celebrated on the Full moon day (Purnima) of Phalgun Month. It is popularly known as the festival of Colors.
Celebrated on the New moon day (Amavasya) of Kartika Month. It is celebrated to mark the return of Lord Rama to Ayodhya after 14 years of exile.
Major spiritual gathering. It is held at four Tirthas: Prayagraj, Haridwar, Nasik, and Ujjain. These are the places where four drops of amrit (nectar) fell during a scuffle between gods and demons.
It signifies the conclusion of Ramadan and is observed by Muslims with fasting, prayers, and communal feasts.
Known as Khichdi.

It is a major festival of Bihar and UP dedicated to "Chhathi Maiya" and the Sun God (Surya). It begins exactly on the 6th day after Diwali. It is a 4-day long festival celebrated during the Kartik month (around October/November).
New Year
It is celebrated with the immersion of elaborately decorated clay idols of Goddess Durga.
Also known as Dol Jatra.
Erok Sim & Magh Sim Festivals. The Santhal community is mainly found in the states of Jharkhand, Bihar, Odisha, and West Bengal.
Known as Poush Sankranti.

It is a 9-day floral festival celebrated mainly by women. A large central arrangement of flowers (called Bathukamma) is made. It starts on Mahalaya Amavasya (New Moon day). Goddess Gauri and nature are worshipped during this festival. It takes place during September-October. Celebrated in Telangana and parts of Andhra Pradesh.

It started in 1813 to eradicate the plague (caused by Yersinia pestis bacteria). A "Bonam" (food offering) is offered to Goddess Mahakali. It is mainly celebrated in Hyderabad and Secunderabad, and was declared the Official State Festival of Telangana in 2014. Potharaju, the brother of Goddess Mahakali, is also worshipped.
Also known as Medaram Jatara. Rituals of this festival are performed by the Koya tribe.
Also Known as Sadar festival. Celebrated by the Yadava Community.
It is celebrated for four days with the Bhogi bonfire.
It signifies the start of the harvest season and the official start of the New Year.

It involves a ritual bath in the river and a procession of deities to purify sins and protect against evil spirits. It involves worship of 14 specific deities. It lasts for 7 days in the month of July. It is mainly celebrated in Agartala (the capital of Tripura).
Celebrated by the Reang community to worship Goddess Mailuma (Laxmi).
It involves traditional tribal dances and rituals after jhum cultivation.
Celebrated by the Chakma tribe to celebrate the New Year.

It is celebrated in Tripura to honor Baba Garia. The "Ochai" acts as a guide or priest for the entire festival. It involves the worship of a bamboo pole. It is celebrated during the month of Chaitra (March-April) and lasts for about 7 days.

It is celebrated at the Hemis Monastery in Ladakh. It takes place during the months of June-July. It is celebrated to commemorate the birth anniversary of Guru Padmasambhava. The famous mask dance known as "Cham" is performed by monks during this festival.
Losar is the Ladakhi New Year. During this festival, symbolic dough models of the Sun, the Moon, and the Ibex (a type of mountain animal) are placed in households to welcome the new year.

Similar to Sikkim's "Saga Dawa". It is celebrated in Ladakh around May-June. It is known as a "Triple Blessed Festival" because it commemorates three major events of Lord Buddha: his birth, his enlightenment (Nirvana), and his death (Mahaparinirvana).
It takes place at the Lamayuru monastery in Ladakh in the months of July-August. It is a 2-day festival where the Mask Dance (Chham) is performed.
Festival of Scapegoats.
It is celebrated at Dilli Haat (Janakpuri) in Delhi. It started in 1987. It typically takes place in the month of July, where more than 1000 varieties of mangoes are showcased.
It is celebrated to honor the village goddess Sengazhuneer Amman. It is a 6-day annual event held in the month of August. A major highlight of this festival is the "car dragging ceremony".

important: Makar Sankranti is celebrated across India, marking the sun's northward movement (Uttarayan), entering the Capricorn zodiac (Makar) at the winter solstice.
It involves fasting, prayer, and self-reflection and is observed during the Bhadrapada month. It is a Jain festival. It is celebrated in the month of Bhadrapada (August-September).
It commemorates the martyrdom of Guru Arjan Dev. Guru Arjan Dev was the 5th Sikh Guru. He was executed by the Mughal Emperor Jahangir for giving shelter to Jahangir's son, Khusrau.
It commemorates the three major life events of Lord Buddha: his birth, his enlightenment, and his death (Mahaparinirvana), also called the "Thrice Blessed Festival."
Major spiritual gathering. It is held at four Tirthas: Prayagraj, Haridwar, Nasik, and Ujjain. These are the places where four drops of amrit (nectar) fell during a scuffle between gods and demons.
It is celebrated as a day of devotion to Lord Shiva and falls on the 14th day of the dark half of the Hindu month Phalguna.
It is a festival observed with fasting by married women for their husbands' well-being, typically celebrated in the Hindu month of Kartik.
It commemorates Guru Hargobind's release with 52 kings.
It is celebrated by the Parsi (Zoroastrian) community. Balban started the Navroz festival in India.
Asia's largest tulip festival is organized in Srinagar.
Celebrated on the New moon day (Amavasya) of Kartika Month. It is celebrated to mark the return of Lord Rama to Ayodhya after 14 years of exile.
Celebrated on the Full moon day (Purnima) of Phalgun Month. It is popularly known as the festival of Colors.
It is celebrated by Kashmiri Pandits. It is celebrated on the first day of the Chaitra month, making it the Kashmiri New Year. Items like walnuts, almonds, and raisins are kept during this festival.
It is a popular festival of North India, and is mainly associated with Sugarcane harvesting.
It signifies the conclusion of Ramadan and is observed by Muslims with fasting, prayers, and communal feasts.
It commemorates the birth anniversary of Prophet Muhammad, observed on the 12th day (Barah Wafat) of Rabi' al-Awwal.
Charity is given during this festival.
